description: Day 2 Stream 2 talks from BSides Las Vegas 2021.

talks.title: All Software is Open Source: An Introduction to Reverse Engineering
talks.teaser: Introduces reverse engineering concepts, legal considerations, tooling and a self-study path for analyzing closed-source software.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by describing reverse engineering as working out how a device, system or program functions by examining it, a practice much older than software. It outlines modern uses such as vulnerability research, penetration testing, malware analysis and building compatible products. The speaker then covers the legal gray area, noting that license terms, statutes such as the DMCA, and the intent behind the work all matter, and separates activities into lower-risk and riskier categories.

The middle section covers technique. Analysts can start with data and network analysis, move on to disassembly and decompilation, and combine static analysis with dynamic debugging. A small C program shows how machine code maps back to source, and Java and .NET are presented as far easier to recover than native binaries. Tools including IDA Pro, Binary Ninja and radare-based frameworks are surveyed, followed by the obstacles analysts meet: compiler optimization, obfuscation, packing, encryption and anti-debugging.

The closing section offers a self-study path, starting with small programs written by the learner, then crackme challenges, then CTF competitions, with the Flare-On contest as the hardest rung. Practical advice includes targeting one specific goal rather than the whole program, using magic numbers and library calls as anchors, and documenting findings as you go. The speaker ends with examples of hard-coded or weakly encoded credentials and a vendor backdoor found in a binary, arguing that developers should not assume compiled code stays hidden.

talks.title: Your critical system IS (NOT?) vulnerable: CSAF, VEX, SBOM and the future of advisories
talks.teaser: Explains how SBOM, VEX and CSAF can communicate whether a product is actually affected by a known vulnerability.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a common problem: when a vulnerability makes headlines, organisations struggle to answer whether their own products or systems are affected. The speakers note that CVE identifiers give everyone a shared name for a flaw, but they say nothing about what to do, and many fixes never receive a CVE. They explain a software bill of materials as a dependency graph listing each component, its supplier, version and identifiers, and stress that this data must be machine readable.

The middle of the talk focuses on VEX, a way for a supplier to state that a product is not affected by a particular vulnerability. Reasons can include the vulnerable code being absent or unreachable. The speakers describe the current advisory process as manual and inconsistent, with advisories in mixed formats and scattered across portals, which overloads the teams that must read and prioritise them. They present CSAF, a JSON-based standard for advisories, with VEX defined as a profile within it, so tooling can match an SBOM against published statements.

The closing section covers the chicken-and-egg problem: vendors are slow to publish machine-readable data unless customers ask for it, and customers cannot ask until it exists. The speakers point to government procurement requirements and European legislation as drivers, and to open-source CSAF tools for creating and validating documents as early but still rough. Practitioners are encouraged to adopt the format, build tooling, and treat publishing not-affected statements as a way to cut support calls and free experts for decisions that need judgement.

talks.title: Secure your AWS accounts without breaking the bank
talks.teaser: Covers ways to secure AWS accounts while keeping costs low.

talks.title: Securing and Trusting Third-Party Javascripts in Your Web App
talks.teaser: Explains the risks of third-party JavaScript in web apps and how CSP, iframes and SRI mitigate them.
talks.summary:
The talk starts by defining third-party JavaScript as code served from external servers that a site owner does not write or control, such as analytics, advertising and social sharing widgets. It then covers the three common ways these scripts reach a page: a direct script tag pointing at a vendor URL, vendor code pasted inline, and loading everything through a tag manager. Tag managers are popular with marketing teams because they let non-developers add or change scripts without redeploying the app.

The talk then turns to risk. A script running in the page gets full access to the DOM, can read sensitive input such as payment details, and can be changed by its owner at any time. The card-skimming attacks against shared checkout scripts show how compromising one vendor can expose many sites at once. Mitigations discussed include a Content Security Policy with script-source directives and nonces, which limits what loads but does not inspect what a script does; an iframe, which blocks DOM access but breaks analytics and tag managers that need the page; and Subresource Integrity, which pins a script to a hash. SRI fits poorly with tag managers, since their containers change without a code deploy and the hash goes stale.

The closing advice is practical. Keep scripts off sensitive pages such as checkout or password change where possible, teach teams that use tag managers about the risks, and bring in vendor security and legal reviews before trusting a provider. When a dynamic script must touch the DOM, the remaining risk is assessed, CSP is used as a baseline, and what is left is formally accepted.

talks.title: Stupid Job Posts Don't Matter!
talks.teaser: Shows how to research employers behind poor job postings and turn confusing requirements into questions that move a job search forward.
talks.summary:
Kirsten Renner opens by saying poorly written job postings frustrate many people, and that a large share of the hacking community reports trouble finding work. She frames the search as an engineering problem: gather requirements, identify blockers, and design solutions. Her first step is to read a posting as a signal of what a company needs, then look past its marketing. Checking who holds the same title on LinkedIn and what employees publicly say about growth and daily work can show whether a role offers room to develop.

She then walks through typical problems: contradictory entry-level requirements, vague terms like "strong," long tool lists lumped together, and postings written for one specific person. Offensive postings, she says, are a reason to walk away. Candidates should turn their doubts into written questions, ask recruiters to answer them, and raise topics such as training, certification costs, and growth plans. When a requirement is missing, describe equivalent experience instead.

The question-and-answer segment covered reaching hiring managers when recruiters go silent, following up after interviews, and asking for feedback that companies may be unable to give. Tailored resumes matter because many employers filter applications by keywords, and a short opening note explaining the goal helps a reader. The takeaway: a weak posting may still point to a good employer, so review it before skipping, and invest in relationships with recruiters.

talks.title: Aristotle In Security: How an Ancient Greek Can Improve Your Security Program
talks.teaser: Applies ideas from Aristotle's philosophy to how a security program is planned and run.

talks.title: Breaking The Giants With Logic
talks.teaser: Shows how business logic flaws in web apps, like invite and reset flows, let attackers bypass intended rules.
talks.summary:
The talk frames business logic vulnerabilities as flaws that do not trigger errors or crashes, but instead let people use a feature in ways its designers never intended. The speaker argues that common automated tooling produces duplicate findings in bug bounty programs, so researchers benefit from reasoning about what a feature is supposed to do. A simple example is an e-commerce checkout where a client-supplied price parameter is changed before the order is submitted.

The middle of the talk walks through several cases. A password reset link carrying a sequential user ID let an attacker reset another account's password despite a strong token. Invitation links were next: altering group or sender identifiers, member type values, or reusing an invite could allow joining restricted groups, impersonating an inviter, or escalating privileges. Two case studies followed. In Facebook groups, a preview state kept a user hidden from admins while retaining rejoin access, and a removed feature's backend still accepted requests. On Instagram, a blocked account could still be followed, letting the user watch content unseen.

The closing advice is to use an application as a regular user before automating, learn which features and controls are weak, and read disclosed reports. Patterns found on one platform often recur on others, which motivates the speaker's plan to build a tool for hunting invitation-style flaws. The Q&A touched on whether stored invitations could enable denial of service, judged an unlikely edge case, and on how often backend remnants of removed features remain reachable.

talks.title: Finance Industry Career Search Panel
talks.teaser: Panelists share how they built security careers in finance, learned its regulations, and what newcomers should expect.
talks.summary:
A panel of finance-sector security professionals, guided by a Higher Ground host, describes how each of them reached their current role. Their routes ran through programming, penetration testing, Big Four consulting, internal audit and application security, with moves in and out of banking, consulting and cloud. They describe a career as a set of lateral moves rather than a straight ladder, with each step teaching something useful.

The discussion then turns to regulation. Early in their careers requirements were sparse, but they grew after the mid-2000s with card-industry standards, the 2008 financial crisis and later international regimes. Learning the rules was usually done as needed, on the job. The panelists point to the sector's broad vocabulary of risk, its conservative and sometimes confrontational culture, and the need to translate technical findings for auditors and executives. Business understanding, relationship building and delivering unwelcome news came up repeatedly as core skills.

For advancement, the speakers advised stretching beyond comfort zones, building relationships outside one's own team, and separating mentors from sponsors. They also suggested being bold about taking on roles, self-promotion without boasting, and negotiating pay firmly. The takeaway for practitioners is that a technical background transfers well into finance, and that the sector rewards people who can connect security work to business objectives.

talks.title: Quad Block Quiz - Supply Chain Sandbox Edition
talks.teaser: Presents a browser game that mixes falling-block puzzle play with trivia on software supply chain security.
talks.summary:
Duncan Sparrell presents Quad Block Quiz, a browser game that mixes falling-block puzzle play with trivia about software supply chain security. Unresolved vulnerabilities and licensing problems clog the board, and too many vulnerabilities trigger attacks that drain the score. Answering questions, whose background text holds the answers, earns power-ups that clear or move blocks, each tied to a supply chain concept.

Next he argues that history matters for this problem. He traces Roman military logistics, nineteenth-century engineering, and his father's work on bridges, insurance loss prevention and early automotive crash safety. From that he argues that software bills of materials are worth creating once risk is measured quantitatively, and he outlines how standards such as CSAF, VEX, OpenC2 and CACAO could automate defense and shorten attacker dwell time.

He closes by describing the game's build in Elixir and Phoenix, its open-source MIT license and its own published SBOM. His main takeaway is that no single fix solves supply chain risk; SBOMs, automation and information sharing have to work together. In questions he discusses SBOM adoption in finance and healthcare, how deep an inventory should go, and combining build-time and post-build scanning.

talks.title: Healthcare Industry Career Search Panel
talks.teaser: Two healthcare security practitioners describe how they entered the field and what skills help newcomers succeed there.
talks.summary:
This Higher Ground panel at BSides Las Vegas 2021 brought together two healthcare security practitioners to talk about building careers in the sector. The moderator opened by asking how each panelist arrived in the field. One came from health policy and privacy work and became a lawyer focused on health data. The other started as a penetration tester and vulnerability researcher, later worked on medical device security at a large manufacturer, and eventually founded a company that serves healthcare providers.

The middle of the discussion covered what sets healthcare apart. Medical equipment often stays in service for decades and runs older operating systems that cannot easily be patched or loaded with security tools. Regulation of device vendors and electronic health record vendors also differs from other industries, which shapes how risk is managed. The panelists stressed learning how clinical operations, payers and providers, and regulations such as HIPAA actually work, and being patient with colleagues who are not security specialists. They were skeptical about certifications and pointed to professional groups and industry events as better ways to meet the people in the field. They also noted that hospital security teams offer broad early-career experience, and that product security and device research roles are growing.

For newcomers, the advice was to ask practitioners how they run their playbooks and to keep up with news and peer discussion. Experienced security professionals moving into healthcare were urged to learn the business first and stay humble. The panel closed by encouraging listeners to reach out to people already working in the field.
